# Introduction

Find all of this in the repo <https://github.com/zahra-arjm/community_notes>

This PDF made by a quarto document <supplement.qmd>. The quarto file renders the outputs for the full set of RDD results (sensitivity check etc), and also pushes some outputs to  /paper-outputs as a .tex fragments so they can be pulled into overleaf directly.

To see the code which is running you need to open the .qmd file. As a PDF this shows commentary (like this text) and code outputs (in text, and images).

AI declaration: all the words are human-written, all the logic and claims are human endorsed (by TS, so they may contain errors). The code was co-written with using an AI agent, some comments from the agent are left in the code (invisible in the PDF).

## Topline results and v1-v2 chanegs

- Since v1 we adopt a more sophisticated RDD method, fix bugs and are stricter on best practice with respect to causal inference. There is still a positive effect, but it is not significant (confidence bounds overlap an effect of 0).

- A zero-indexing bug meant previously we were looking at the effect of first note status on 3rd note publication. This is now fixed.

- There is (remains) a robust effect for authoring a 3rd note (`have_another_note = note_counts[(note_counts >= 3)]`).

- We discover the RDD is not sharp, due to the fact that we have the score (intercept) from the data cut off point, which is NOT the intercept at the point when the note was or was not published (scores continuing to evolve post publication). This non-sharpness can be dealt with by running a fuzzy-RDD which accounts for the change in probabilities of being published at different intercept scores (there is still a discontinuity in these probailities).

- In addition there is a special population of Notes just below the cutoff threshold (intercept 0.39 - 0.40) which have a high probability of having been published. This is due to a documented *feature* of the CN system, whereby notes are protected from being unpublished when their score drops by a small amount (<0.01). These can be handled by using a "Donut" RDD, where notes +/- 0.01 of the cutoff are excluded 

- To do all of this we move from using OLS to the robust RDD package

- We also run additional sensitivity checks and robustness checks (e.g. local density check around threshold)

```{python}
#| label: functions


def get_first_notes(rated, note_from, note_to, cutoff, *, re_auth_thresh = 2):
    '''function to define data for analysis - running variable, outcome variable, sample defined by date'''

    
    print("ALERT! re_auth_thresh = ", re_auth_thresh)

    ## CHANGED 2026-08-29
    def get_decided_value(row, value_type):
        # a function to map decidedBy values to both factor and intercept
        model = re.sub(r'Model.*$', '', row['decidedBy']).strip()
        model = model[0].lower() + model[1:]
        
        column = f"{model}Note{value_type}"
        return row[column]

    # Find the first note written by each author, and if that author goes on to write another note
    # nb adding sort_values('createdAt') as sanity check, df is mostly pre-sortes

    # OLD versjon - using .first() which is vulnerable to dropping rows with Nans
    # first_notes = rated.sort_values('createdAt').groupby('noteAuthorParticipantId')\
    #     [['createdAt', 'finalRatingStatus', 'numRatings', 'rating_group',
    #     'decidedBy','coreNoteFactor1', 'coreNoteIntercept', 'coreNoteInterceptMax',
    #     'expansionNoteFactor1', 'expansionNoteIntercept', 'expansionNoteInterceptMax',
    #     'coreWithTopicsNoteFactor1', 'coreWithTopicsNoteIntercept', 'coreWithTopicsNoteInterceptMax',
    #     'classification']]\
    #     .first().reset_index()

    # NEW version - using .head(1) which is more robust to Nans
    # CHANGED 2026-08-29 to include expansionPlusNoteFactor1 and expansionPlusNoteIntercept
    cols = ['noteAuthorParticipantId', 'createdAt', 'finalRatingStatus',
        'numRatings', 'rating_group', 'decidedBy',
        'firstNonNMRStatus', 'mostRecentNonNMRStatus', 'lockedStatus','timestampMillisOfFirstNmrDueToMinStableCrhTime',
        'coreNoteFactor1', 'coreNoteIntercept', 'coreNoteInterceptMax',
        'expansionNoteFactor1', 'expansionNoteIntercept', 'expansionNoteInterceptMax',
        'expansionPlusNoteFactor1', 'expansionPlusNoteIntercept',
        'coreWithTopicsNoteFactor1', 'coreWithTopicsNoteIntercept', 'coreWithTopicsNoteInterceptMax',
        'classification']

    first_notes = (rated.sort_values('createdAt')
                    .groupby('noteAuthorParticipantId', sort=False)
                    .head(1)
                    [cols]
                    .reset_index(drop=True))


    print("Now we have " + str(len(first_notes)) + " first time note authors (all time)")
    # Restricting our analysis to authors who joined in 2024 or 2025 
    first_notes = first_notes[(first_notes.createdAt >= note_from) &
                            (first_notes.createdAt <= note_to)]

    print("Now we have " + str(len(first_notes)) + " first time note authors " + note_from.strftime("%Y-%m-%d") + " to " + note_to.strftime("%Y-%m-%d"))
    
    # define outcome variable

    # Restricting our analysis to notes after 2024
    rated_2024 = rated[(rated.createdAt >= pd.Timestamp(2024,1,1))]

    # code by number of authored notes explicitl
    note_counts = rated_2024.groupby('noteAuthorParticipantId').size()
    have_another_note = note_counts[(note_counts >= re_auth_thresh)].index
    
    # cumsum is zero indexed (wtf!) so a score of 1 means the author has written at least 2 notes
    #have_another_note = rated_2024[rated_2024.groupby('noteAuthorParticipantId').cumcount() >= 1]\
    #    ['noteAuthorParticipantId'].to_list()

    

    # add to primary dataframe
    first_notes['if_written_again'] = first_notes['noteAuthorParticipantId'].isin(have_another_note)
    # filter to only notes written by the major algorithms
    # define models (algorithms to include))
    #models = ['CoreModel (v1.1)'] # >70% of Notes,
    #models = ['CoreModel (v1.1)', 'ExpansionModel (v1.1)', 'CoreWithTopicsModel (v1.1)']
    models = ['CoreModel (v1.1)', 'ExpansionModel (v1.1)', 'ExpansionPlusModel (v1.1)', 'CoreWithTopicsModel (v1.1)']
    # select on models
    first_notes = first_notes[first_notes['decidedBy'].isin(models)]
    
    print("Now we have " + str(len(first_notes)) + " notes written by our " + str(len(models)) + " choosen algorithms")

    # remove NNNs
    first_notes = first_notes[first_notes['classification'] != 'NOT_MISLEADING']
    ## NNNs are not misleading, the remainder are classified as misleading
    print("Now we have " + str(len(first_notes)) + " notes classified as MISLEADING")

    # CHANGED 2026-08-29, to use new function (above)
    # adding intercept and factor from the deciding algorithm
    first_notes['intercept'] = first_notes.apply(
        lambda row: get_decided_value(row, 'Intercept'),
        axis=1
    )

    first_notes['factor'] = first_notes.apply(
        lambda row: get_decided_value(row, 'Factor1'),
        axis=1
    )

    # built 'ever_published' variable
    first_notes["ever_published"] = (
        (first_notes.firstNonNMRStatus == "CURRENTLY_RATED_HELPFUL") |
        (first_notes.mostRecentNonNMRStatus == "CURRENTLY_RATED_HELPFUL")
        ).astype(int)



    #Version 1, only keep only notes with enough rating
    #Version 2, only keep notes with >0 ratings
    first_notes = first_notes[first_notes['rating_group'] == 1]
    print("Now we have " + str(len(first_notes)) + " notes which have >0 ratings")

    # keep only aligned notes (current status and final status align)
    if ALIGNMENT:
        mask_alignment = (((first_notes["intercept"] > cutoff) & (first_notes["finalRatingStatus"] == "CURRENTLY_RATED_HELPFUL")) |
            ((first_notes["intercept"] < cutoff) & (first_notes["finalRatingStatus"] != "CURRENTLY_RATED_HELPFUL")))
        # Altrenative
        #mask_alignment = (rated['lockedStatus'].astype(str)!='None') #new
        first_notes = first_notes[mask_alignment]
        print("Now we have " + str(len(first_notes)) + " aligned notes")
    else:
        print("--------         No filter for alignment")

  
    print("FINAL total", len(first_notes), "Notes")
    print("of which author writes again = ", len(first_notes[first_notes['if_written_again']]))
    print(f"\nNB current (final), not Max, score")


    return first_notes

def robust_rdd(x,y,c, *, p = 1, kernel = "triangular", fuzzy = None):
    '''wrapper function to run rdrobust and print results'''
    #
    # declare outinputs
    print("running variable (x) length", len(x))
    print("binary outcome (y) length", len(y))
    print("cutoff (c) is", c)

    # next line is the regression
    fit = rdrobust(y=y, x=x, c=c, p=p, kernel=kernel, fuzzy=fuzzy)
    # now we're just formatting the output
    print(fit)                              # full CCT-style table
    h_mse = float(fit.bws.iloc[0, 0])       # selected h (left; symmetric by default)
    print(f"\nMSE-optimal h = {h_mse:.4f}")

    #report the bias-corrected point estimate with the robust 95% CI
    print(f"\nBias-corrected point estimate: {fit.coef.iloc[1, 0]:.4f}  "
        f"95% CI [{fit.ci.iloc[2, 0]:.4f}, {fit.ci.iloc[2, 1]:.4f}]")

    # --- Bandwidth sensitivity: h/2, h, 2h ---
    # Report bias-corrected point + robust 95% CI (rows 1 and 2 of coef/ci).
    print("\nBandwidth sensitivity (bias-corrected point, robust 95% CI):")
    h_mse = float(fit.bws.iloc[0, 0])
    b_mse = float(fit.bws.iloc[1, 0])   # b lives in row 1 of bws
    for mult in (0.5, 1.0, 2.0):
        h=h_mse*mult
        b= b_mse*mult # b and h covary so that rho stays fixed (as dervied from intial fit)
        r = rdrobust(y=y, x=x, c=c, p=p, kernel=kernel, fuzzy=fuzzy,
                    h=h, b=b)
        tau  = float(r.coef.iloc[0, 0]) # note that tau is for the conventional model
        lo   = float(r.ci.iloc[2, 0]) #but the CI is for the robust model
        hi   = float(r.ci.iloc[2, 1])
        nL, nR = int(r.N_h[0]), int(r.N_h[1])
        print(f"  h = {h:.4f} ({mult:.1f}x)  tau = {tau:+.4f}  "
            f"95% CI [{lo:+.4f}, {hi:+.4f}]  N_L/N_R = {nL}/{nR}")

    return fit

```

We fix the cumsum=>2 issue, so we have authors who write 2 (not 3) notes as our outcome variable
We also remove the alignment filter, since this is conditioning on a collider (and makes our RDD artificially sharp)

Sadly, though, our data record intercept calculated from the full set of ratings, this is not the contemporanious intercept score which determines moment-by-moment publication. It approximates it, but with contamination. Notes may be published then unpublished as they receive more ratings and their rating degrades, or there may be additional blocks on publication (e.g. requirements on total number or type of ratings, or requirements on intercept stability or a lag before publication). The CN system is not entirely clear about all these details.

These contamination can be seen by plotting indicators of ever having been published against our (final) intercept.

We construct an independent 'ever_published' variable from the `firstNonNMRStatus` and `mostRecentNonNMRStatus` variables. The logic being that if either of these are `CURRENTLY_RATED_HELPFUL` then the Note must have achieved CRH/published status at some point in the past (ie seperate from the finalRatingStatus score)

This shows that our secondary indicator of publication status shows a discontinuity near the cutoff, but not a sharp one

The high proportion of 'ever published' just below the cutoff suggests many notes got published and then slipped back below the threshold

We deal with this by a) using a fuzzy RDD and b) excluding the just below cutoff points by using the donut method


# Trad OLS RDD

Our first approach was to use OLS and an arbitary window

This is now signficant with a wide window (0.08, it was non-significant at 0.05), and a 0.01 donut (but not significant if donut = 0, because of the contamination in the 0.39-0.40 zone))

```{python}
#| label: OLS-RDD

bandwidth = 0.08 #window around cutoff
print("bandwidth = ", bandwidth)
DONUT = 0.01 # exluding notes near cutoff, we'll change later

# data for OLS RDD
running_variable = first_notes['intercept']
treatment = np.where(running_variable >= CUTOFF, 1, 0)
outcome_variable = first_notes['if_written_again'].astype(int)
# we only fit data within the window
mask = (running_variable > CUTOFF - bandwidth)  & (running_variable < CUTOFF + bandwidth)
donut_mask = (first_notes['intercept'] - CUTOFF).abs() >= DONUT
data = pd.DataFrame({
    'running_variable': running_variable[mask & donut_mask],
    'treatment': treatment[mask & donut_mask],
    'outcome_variable': outcome_variable[mask & donut_mask]
})

# Center the running variable at the cutoff for easier interpretation of the intercept
data['running_variable_centered'] = data['running_variable'] - CUTOFF
print(f"\nNumber of treated units: {data['treatment'].sum()}")
print(f"Number of control units: {data['treatment'].count() - data['treatment'].sum()}")

# original
rdd_model_formula = 'outcome_variable ~ running_variable_centered * treatment'

# Without data sanitisation this doesn't run
if False:
    rdd_model = smf.ols(formula=rdd_model_formula, data=data).fit()

# data inspection
data['running_variable_centered'].dtype # dtype('O') <- problem!

# but each individual value is a float
data['running_variable_centered'].apply(type).value_counts()

# let's just convert to float
data = data.astype({'running_variable_centered': float})

# Now the RDD runs
if True:
    rdd_model = smf.ols(formula=rdd_model_formula, data=data).fit()
# # assuming the model runs you can run the rest


# The coefficient for 'treatment' is the estimated effect at the cutoff.
estimated_effect = rdd_model.params['treatment']
print(f"\nEstimated Treatment Effect at the Cutoff: {estimated_effect:.4f}")

print("I think we can intepret this as a % change the chance of authoring again if published")

p_value_treatment = rdd_model.pvalues['treatment']
t_statistic_treatment = rdd_model.tvalues['treatment']

# print out p value and t-statistic for treatment
print(f"\nP-value for treatment: {p_value_treatment:.4f}")
print(f"T-statistic for treatment: {t_statistic_treatment:.4f}")

```

This OLS approach provides a bridge to the fuzzy-RDD approach, which uses robust RDD to esimate the window size (as well as bringing in a bunch of statistical machinery which is best practice for RDDs)

# RDD using fuzzy rdrobust with a donut 

The rdrobust function will estimate the bandwidth from the data, as well as provide various sensitivity checks and allow a fuzzy RDD

It has the option of using a polynomial fit (which we decline), and uses all points, weigted by proximity to cutoff

We are using a 'donut' method of excluding those points near the cutoff, this is specifically to get those points just below the cutoff which have a high (outlier) percentage change of ever having been published

References for this method

@article{calonico2014robust,
  title   = {Robust Nonparametric Confidence Intervals for Regression-Discontinuity Designs},
  author  = {Calonico, Sebastian and Cattaneo, Matias D. and Titiunik, Rocio},
  journal = {Econometrica},
  volume  = {82},
  number  = {6},
  pages   = {2295--2326},
  year    = {2014},
  doi     = {10.3982/ECTA11757}
}

@article{calonico2018effect,
  title   = {On the Effect of Bias Estimation on Coverage Accuracy in Nonparametric Inference},
  author  = {Calonico, Sebastian and Cattaneo, Matias D. and Farrell, Max H.},
  journal = {Journal of the American Statistical Association},
  volume  = {113},
  number  = {522},
  pages   = {767--779},
  year    = {2018},
  doi     = {10.1080/01621459.2017.1285776}
}

@article{calonico2014rdrobust,
  title   = {Robust Data-Driven Inference in the Regression-Discontinuity Design},
  author  = {Calonico, Sebastian and Cattaneo, Matias D. and Titiunik, Rocio},
  journal = {The Stata Journal},
  volume  = {14},
  number  = {4},
  pages   = {909--946},
  year    = {2014},
  doi     = {10.1177/1536867X1401400413}
}

Justifying the donut RDD, we can test if intercept (our running variable) is associated with 'ever published'


```{python}
#| label: RDD-robust-fuzzy-justification

# --- First stage: does crossing c = 0.4 move publication probability? ---
DONUT_PRIMARY = 0.01
DONUT_VARIATIONS = [0.0, 0.005, 0.02]

fn = first_notes[["intercept", "ever_published"]].dropna().copy()
fn["ever_published"] = fn["ever_published"].astype(float)

def first_stage(d):
    sample = fn[(fn.intercept - CUTOFF).abs() >= d]
    return rdrobust(
        y=sample.ever_published, x=sample.intercept,
        c=CUTOFF, p=POLY, kernel=KERNEL, bwselect="mserd", all=True,
    )

print(f"PRIMARY SPEC — donut ±{DONUT_PRIMARY}")
print(first_stage(DONUT_PRIMARY))

for d in DONUT_VARIATIONS:
    print(f"\n- - - - variation: donut ±{d}")
    print(first_stage(d))




```


So this is saying that if you exclude at 0 (no exclusions) or 0.005 our running variable isn't cleanly associated with "ever published" (at 0.0 coefficient is close to zero (and n.s). at 0.05 it is negative (and n.s.). At 0.01 the effect is positive and robust (significant), so this justifies the donut

The flip in significance shows significant contamination at the cutoff (those just below *more* likely to be ever published than those just above!). So the justification for the donut is not just that it excludes problematic points, but the RDD is only possible against a background of linear stablitity (which would not exist without the donut).

Note also the negligable drop in N with donut 0.01. We're not losing too much data this way.

We can visualise the donut, and this in particular provides the justification (showing that our contamination of high p(ever_published) Notes below the cutoff is particularly high in the 0.39-0.40)

```{python}
#| label: RDD-donut-visualisation

# --- Publication rate by intercept, close-up on the cutoff ---
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

WINDOW = 0.03    # plot range: ±0.03 around cutoff
BIN_W  = 0.002   # bin width
DONUT  = 0.01    # primary-spec exclusion band

near  = fn[(fn.intercept - CUTOFF).abs() <= WINDOW].copy()
edges = np.arange(CUTOFF - WINDOW, CUTOFF + WINDOW + BIN_W / 2, BIN_W)
near["bin"] = pd.cut(near.intercept, edges)

binned = near.groupby("bin", observed=True).agg(
    mid=("intercept", "mean"),
    pub_rate=("ever_published", "mean"),
    n=("ever_published", "size"),
)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4.5))
ax.axvspan(CUTOFF - DONUT, CUTOFF + DONUT, color="grey", alpha=0.20,
           label=f"donut ±{DONUT} (excluded in primary spec)")
ax.axvline(CUTOFF, color="black", lw=0.8, ls="--")
ax.scatter(binned.mid, binned.pub_rate, s=np.sqrt(binned.n) * 2,
           color="C0", zorder=3)
ax.set_xlabel("Final intercept score")
ax.set_ylabel("P(ever published)")
ax.set_ylim(-0.02, 1.02)
ax.legend(frameon=False, loc="upper left")
plt.show()

# '''Mephi:
# Why: the platform has a documented hysteresis rule of exactly 0.01. I just pulled the open-source scorer (github.com/twitter/communitynotes):
# crhThreshold = 0.40 and inertiaDelta = 0.01 — scoring/src/scoring/mf_base_scorer.py:178,188
# AddCRHInertia rule: a note that is already CRH keeps its status while its intercept stays within [crhThreshold − inertiaDelta, crhThreshold) — i.e. [0.39, 0.40). Class in scoring_rules.py:1521, docstring literally says "notes with intercepts in a defined range (e.g. 0.01 below the general threshold)"; instantiated with crhThreshold - inertiaDelta in note_ratings.py:771.
# So the [0.39, 0.40) plateau is published notes whose scores sagged after publication but whose status is being held up by the inertia rule. Below 0.39 the inertia protection ends, the plateau collapses — hence the sharp break your plot shows precisely at the grey band's left edge.
# '''

```

So this shows the operation fo the inertiaDelta = 0.01 rule, see scoring_rules.py line 1521. Notes which are published and drop 0.01 or less keep their status `https://github.com/twitter/communitynotes/blob/main/scoring/src/scoring/scoring_rules.py`

The OLS serves as a sanity check, but now let's run the full fuzzy RDD 


```{python}
#| label: RDD-robust-fuzzy
# pip install rdrobust # or update conda env


DONUT = 0.01 # ie exclude notes near the cutoff
donut_mask = (first_notes['intercept'] - CUTOFF).abs() >= DONUT
fuzzy_sample = first_notes[donut_mask]
y=fuzzy_sample['if_written_again'].astype(int)
x=fuzzy_sample['intercept']

fit = robust_rdd(y=y, x=x,c=CUTOFF,
    p=POLY, kernel=KERNEL,
    fuzzy=fuzzy_sample.ever_published,
    )

```

This is positive but non-significant

# Converting rate to baseline outcome rate

```{python}
#| label: reporting percentages

h_mse = float(fit.bws.iloc[0, 0])       # selected h (left; symmetric by default)
tau = float(fit.coef.iloc[0, 0])        # note that tau is for the conventional model
p_rob = fit.pv.iloc[2,0]
ci_lo = float(fit.ci.iloc[2, 0]) #CI is for the robust model
ci_hi = float(fit.ci.iloc[2, 1])

base_all = y.mean()
mask_local = (x >= 0.4 - h_mse) & (x < 0.4)
base_local = y[mask_local].mean()

treated_local = base_local + tau
rel_lift = tau / base_local

```

```{python}
#| label: reduced form

# --- Step 5: reduced form / ITT alongside the fuzzy LATE (same donut sample) ---
# x, y, c and d (treatment = publication indicator) are the SAME vectors
# used in the fuzzy headline call. d is what you passed as fuzzy=... there.

# 1. Fuzzy LATE — grab its MSE-optimal bandwidth so the three rows are comparable
late = rdrobust(y=y, x=x, c=CUTOFF, fuzzy=fuzzy_sample.ever_published)
h = float(late.bws.loc["h", "left"])           # common bandwidth for the tie-out

# 2. Reduced form / ITT: sharp RDD of the OUTCOME on x (no fuzzy), at common h
rf = rdrobust(y=y, x=x, c=CUTOFF, h=h, b=h)

# 3. First stage: sharp RDD of TREATMENT on x, at the same h
fs = rdrobust(y=fuzzy_sample.ever_published, x=x, c=CUTOFF, h=h, b=h)

def row(res):
    coef = float(res.coef.loc["Conventional"].iloc[0])
    ci   = res.ci.loc["Robust"]
    return coef, float(ci.iloc[0]), float(ci.iloc[1])

rf_c, rf_lo, rf_hi = row(rf)
fs_c, fs_lo, fs_hi = row(fs)
la_c, la_lo, la_hi = row(late)

print(f"Common bandwidth h = {h:.4f}\n")
print(f"Reduced form (ITT):  {rf_c:+.4f}  robust CI [{rf_lo:+.4f}, {rf_hi:+.4f}]")
print(f"First stage:         {fs_c:+.4f}  robust CI [{fs_lo:+.4f}, {fs_hi:+.4f}]")
print(f"Fuzzy LATE:          {la_c:+.4f}  robust CI [{la_lo:+.4f}, {la_hi:+.4f}]")
print(f"\nTie-out check:  RF / FS = {rf_c/fs_c:+.4f}   (should ≈ LATE at common h)")





```


The RD robust method identifies a MSE-optimal bandwidth of h = `{python} f"{h_mse:.3f}"`), and provides an estimated treatmennt effect of  ↓ 
$\hat{\tau}$ = `{python} f"{tau:+.3f}"`. This is reflects `{python} f"{tau*100:+.1f}"`percentage point increase in the probability of writing a second note if an author's first note is published (conventional local-linear estimator; robust bias-corrected 95% CI
[`{python} f"{ci_lo*100:+.1f}"`, `{python} f"{ci_hi*100:+.1f}"`],
p = `{python} f"{p_rob:.2f}"`). Calonico et al., 2014

The rate of republishing for Notes which fall before the cutoff is ~`{python} f"{base_local:.1%}"`. The treatment effect of `{python} f"{tau*100:.1f}"`pp, imnplies a `{python} f"{rel_lift:.1%}"` relative lift over the counterfactual baseline, however this difference is non-significant.

Now with the local-lineat fits (over the rdrobust defined window), which more accurately represents what the model is doing

```{python}
#| label: RDD-robust-plot-matplotlib

# Matplot lib version of figure

# use rdplot to get parameters, which we're going to redraw in matplotlib
out = rdplot(y=y, x=x, c=CUTOFF, kernel=KERNEL,
             binselect='es', ci=95, hide=True)

b, pl = out.vars_bins, out.vars_poly

# we also need to re-derive the regessions using the triangular kernel
def local_line(side_mask):
    xs, ys = x[side_mask], y[side_mask]
    kw = 1 - np.abs(xs - CUTOFF) / h_mse
    b1, b0 = np.polyfit(xs, ys, 1, w=np.sqrt(kw))
    grid = np.linspace(xs.min(), xs.max(), 50)
    return grid, b0 + b1 * grid, (b0, b1)

gl, vl, (b0l, b1l) = local_line((x >= CUTOFF - h_mse) & (x < CUTOFF))
gr, vr, (b0r, b1r) = local_line((x >= CUTOFF) & (x <= CUTOFF + h_mse))

# triangular-kernel weight of each bin midpoint (0 outside the window)
w = np.clip(1 - np.abs(b.rdplot_mean_x - CUTOFF) / h_mse, 0, 1)
sizes = 8 + 60 * w          # floor of 8 so out-of-window bins stay visible

fig, ax = plt.subplots()

ax.errorbar(b.rdplot_mean_x, b.rdplot_mean_y,
            yerr=[b.rdplot_mean_y - b.rdplot_ci_l,
                  b.rdplot_ci_r - b.rdplot_mean_y],
            fmt='none', ecolor='grey', elinewidth=0.8, alpha=0.6)
ax.scatter(b.rdplot_mean_x, b.rdplot_mean_y, s=sizes, color='grey', zorder=3)

ax.plot(gl, vl, 'r-', lw=2) #left
ax.plot(gr, vr, 'r-', lw=2) #right
ax.axvline(CUTOFF, ls='--', color='k', lw=0.8)

ax.set_xlim(left=0.27, right=0.53)
#ax.set_xlim(c - 4*h_mse, c + 4*h_mse) 
ax.set_ylim(0,1)

ax.set_xlabel('note intercept')
ax.set_ylabel('P(author writes again)')
ax.spines[['top', 'right']].set_visible(False)
ax.margins(x=0.02)

fig.savefig(f'{STEM}_mpl.png', dpi=300, bbox_inches='tight')
fig.savefig(f'{STEM}_mpl.pdf', bbox_inches='tight')   # vector, for the paper

plt.show()

print("consistency check: gap at cutoff should ≈ conventional tau")
gap = (b0r + b1r * CUTOFF) - (b0l + b1l * CUTOFF)
print(f"plot gap at c = {gap:+.4f}  vs  conventional tau = {tau:+.4f}")
```




# Robustness check - density test

Next, manipulation test/density smoothness at cutoff. The density test is standard for RDD, to show that nothing weird is happening in *counts* at the cutoff.

This also, incidentally, shows the donut cut

```{python}
#| label: RDD-density

binW = 0.02 #h_mse #0.05 #window around cutoff
print("Inspecting density with a window of +/o = ", binW)

dens = rddensity(X=x, c=CUTOFF, binoW=binW) # binoW forces window to be 0.38 to 0.42, which is a stricter test of balance around threshold

print(dens.test)   # T-stat and p-value; three rows for VCE variants (conventional / TW / jackknife)
print(dens.hat)    # left/right density point estimates and the jump
print(dens.h)      # bandwidths h_L, h_R
print(dens.n)      # effective N on each side within bandwidth
print(dens.bino)   # binomial-count local test at the cutoff (defaults on)

print([a for a in dir(dens) if not a.startswith('_')])

mask = (x >= CUTOFF - binW) & (x <= CUTOFF + binW)
x_near = x[mask]

# Direct matplotlib histogram — most informative
plt.hist(x_near, bins=50, edgecolor='black')
plt.axvline(0.4, color='red', linestyle='--')
plt.xlabel('intercept'); plt.ylabel('count')
plt.show()
```

The density does progressively decrease up to the cutoff, but there are but no signs of sub-threshold notes being shifted to above threshold (decline not matched by leap post-cutoff)




# Robustness check - Donut RDD

We can run the analysis with different size donuts. This isn't really necessary, since our donut size is defined from first principles (the 0.01 hysterisis on Notes getting unpublished), but let's have a look anyway).

```{python}
#| label: RDD-donut


donut_widths = [0, 0.005, 0.010, 0.020]
rows = []

for DONUT in donut_widths:

    donut_mask = (first_notes['intercept'] - CUTOFF).abs() >= DONUT
    fuzzy_sample = first_notes[donut_mask]
    y=fuzzy_sample['if_written_again'].astype(int)
    x=fuzzy_sample['intercept']

    fit = rdrobust(y=y, x=x,c=CUTOFF,
        p=POLY, kernel=KERNEL,
        fuzzy=fuzzy_sample.ever_published,
        )

    rows.append({
        "donut": f"±{DONUT:.3f}",
        "n_eff_L": int(fit.N_h[0]),
        "n_eff_R": int(fit.N_h[1]),
        "h": round(float(fit.bws.iloc[0, 0]), 3),
        "coef_conv": round(float(fit.coef.iloc[0, 0]), 4),
        "se_conv":   round(float(fit.se.iloc[0, 0]),   4),
        "p_robust":  round(float(fit.pv.iloc[2, 0]),   4),
        "ci_robust_lo": round(float(fit.ci.iloc[2, 0]), 4),
        "ci_robust_hi": round(float(fit.ci.iloc[2, 1]), 4),
    })

df = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print(df.to_string(index=False))
```

This shows that the effect never gets significant at any donut width (ie the non-effect is robust). You can see also that the donut = 0 row is aberant (coefficient has negative sign), which is due to the contamination which justified a non-zero donut in the first place

# Sensitivity check - RDD sensitivity with different cutoffs

Only a cutoff of 0.4 makes sense in terms of the CN publication mechanism. Therefore we expect other thresholds to show no effect (definitely below 0.4, cutoffs above 0.4 will include some published notes above and below that cutoffs, so if there is a true effect may report an attenuated form of that. We can adjust for this by running the RDD on the data above 0.4 only for tresholds above 0.4)


```{python}
#| label: RDD-sensitivity-cutoff
DONUT = 0.01 
donut_mask = (first_notes['intercept'] - CUTOFF).abs() >= DONUT
fuzzy_sample = first_notes[donut_mask]
y=fuzzy_sample['if_written_again'].astype(int)
x=fuzzy_sample['intercept']



c=0.3;robust_rdd(x,y,c) # all ns and inconsistent effect directions
c=0.35;robust_rdd(x,y,c) # all ns and inconsistent effect directions
mask=x>0.4
c=0.45;robust_rdd(x[mask],y[mask],c) # all ns and inconsistent effect directions

```

0.3 and 0.35 are non-significant and the effect esimates are close to zero

the 0.45 cutoff is significant, but the derived bandwidth is too small to be robust, suggesting degenerate model fitting
